title: Protocol Tunneling
summary: Protocol tunneling wraps one protocol inside another so that traffic can pass through filters or reach systems that are not directly routable. The outer carrier is usually something the network already permits, such as Secure Shell (SSH), HTTPS or the Domain Name System (DNS), while the inner traffic is whatever the operator needs, which may include Server Message Block (SMB), Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) or an internal web application. Because the wrapper is encrypted or looks like normal business traffic, flow records show a long lived session to one address rather than many separate connections. Detection rests on shape and volume: an SSH session that moves far more data than an interactive login, DNS queries with unusually large or repetitive answers, or HTTPS to a host that no user on that segment should be contacting. The technique is often combined with a proxy so the true destination stays hidden.

beginner.definition: Tunneling means hiding one kind of network traffic inside another kind. It is like sending a letter inside a parcel. The outside looks ordinary, so filters let it pass. Attackers use tunnels to reach systems that are otherwise blocked.
beginner.whyItMatters: Firewalls often block traffic that is not needed. A tunnel lets blocked traffic travel inside allowed traffic. The hidden data can carry commands or stolen files. Because the outer traffic is allowed, your rules may not stop it. You need to look at the shape of the traffic, not only the port.
howItWorks: The attacker sets up a tunnel between their system and a computer inside the network.
One protocol carries the other, so the inner traffic travels inside the outer one.
Secure Shell supports port forwarding, which moves other traffic through the session.
Domain name queries can hide data inside HTTPS, a method called DNS over HTTPS.
The tunnel can also route traffic that the network would normally drop.
Long sessions with a steady data flow are what the logs actually show.
beginner.example: Think of a border crossing with strict rules about goods. A lorry carrying sealed boxes is waved through because the paperwork says it holds office supplies. Inside one box is something quite different. The guards checked the lorry, not every box. Network tunnels work in the same way. The outer traffic looks allowed, so filters pass it. Security teams learn to weigh the boxes and to watch for lorries that return every day.
takeaways: Allowed traffic can still carry something you would block.
Watch session length and data volume, not only the port number.
Unexpected DNS or HTTPS patterns are worth a closer look.

objectives: Explain what it means to encapsulate one protocol inside another.
Describe why tunneling defeats filtering that is based on ports.
Recognise tunneling indicators in flow records and DNS logs.
Explain how tunnels support later stages such as command and control.
Compare a malicious tunnel with a legitimate virtual private network.
